answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine passage from the ‘Tao Te Ching’ (Dao De Jing), Chapter 17, the classic traditionally attributed to Lao Tzu. The exact English wording is James Legge’s 1891 translation (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 39); the popular version simply drops Legge’s bracketed insertions such as ‘(the people)’ and ‘(their rulers).’

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Tâo Teh King (Tao Te Ching / Dao De Jing), Chapter 17
James Legge, 1891 — Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 39

source.excerpt: In the highest antiquity, (the people) did not know that there were (their rulers). In the next age they loved them and praised them. In the next they feared them; in the next they despised them. Thus it was that when faith (in the Tâo) was deficient (in the rulers) a want of faith in them ensued (in the people). How irresolute did those (earliest rulers) appear, showing (by their reticence) the importance which they set upon their words! Their work was done and their undertakings were successful, while the people all said, ‘We are as we are, of ourselves!’
trail: The distinctive phrases — “In the highest antiquity… did not know that there were their rulers” and “We are as we are, of ourselves” — appear verbatim in James Legge’s 1891 rendering of Tao Te Ching, Chapter 17 ↗.
The translation was first published in The Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 39 (1891) ↗, edited by F. Max Müller — placing this English wording firmly in the public domain.
Side-by-side translation compilations confirm the same Legge text and show how other renderings (Bynner, Mitchell, etc.) reword the same chapter at this Chapter-17 collection ↗.
source.excerptNote: Legge’s full Chapter 17, with his bracketed clarifications restored. The circulating quote is this same passage with the brackets removed.

author.bio: Lao Tzu (Laozi, ‘Old Master’) is the semi-legendary Chinese sage traditionally named as the author of the Tao Te Ching, the foundational text of Taoism. Modern scholars debate whether he was a single historical figure or whether the book is a compiled work of the Warring States period, but the text has been credited to him for over two millennia. The precise English wording quoted here belongs to the Scottish sinologist James Legge (1815–1897), whose 1891 rendering remains one of the most widely reproduced.

misattribution.heading: A genuine quote — with a translation caveat
misattribution.intro: Unlike most lines pinned on famous sages, this one is authentic: it really is from the Tao Te Ching, Chapter 17, the work credited to Lao Tzu. The only things worth flagging are how it is framed.

items.who: ‘Lao Tzu’ as a single historical author
items.why: The Tao Te Ching is traditionally attributed to Lao Tzu, but many scholars regard the text as a compiled work and Lao Tzu as a semi-legendary figure. The line is genuinely from the book credited to him — just don’t treat ‘Lao Tzu’ as a documented single speaker.

The elegant English is James Legge’s 1891 translation, not Lao Tzu’s literal words. Popular reposts also quietly delete Legge’s bracketed clarifications (‘(the people)’, ‘(their rulers)’), which is why the circulating text reads more smoothly than the printed original at terebess.hu ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: authentic. It is Tao Te Ching, Chapter 17 ↗, correctly attributed to Lao Tzu, in James Legge’s public-domain 1891 rendering.

context.heading: Why it’s quoted
lead: Chapter 17 is one of the most-cited passages in leadership and management writing. It ranks four kinds of rulers — the best, whose people barely notice them; then the loved; then the feared; then the despised — and closes with the ideal outcome: the work gets done and the people credit themselves.

The final line, “We are as we are, of ourselves,” is the seed of countless modern paraphrases about the invisible leader, most famously Witter Bynner’s and others’ ‘when the work is done… they will say: we did it ourselves.’
context.pull: The best rulers are barely known; their success is one the people claim as their own.
